newsitem.title: USA: Troubled Florida bonds don't signal wide default.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Florida bonds don't signal wide default.

text.p: The bankruptcy filing by the limited partnerships that built waste-to-energy plants in Florida is not a harbinger of widespread default in the municipal solid-waste sector, a report by A.G. Edwards & Sons concluded.
Fixed-income research analyst Patrick Early said the solid waste sector in general, and resource recovery projects in particular, do face new pressure from competition and the loss of flow control.
But he said there are important differences between those plants and traditional municipal solid-waste projects.
Like the troubled Illinois waste-to-energy plants that made headlines last year, the Florida plants were non-rated, profit-minded projects.

They and the Illinois plant were narrowly secured "spec" projects built to take advantage of laws favoring energy generated by waste-to-energy plants. They rely on power sales to utilities using "avoided cost" rates.
"It allows these alternative power plants to make money at retail rates, typically at or above market rates," Early told Reuters in a phone interview.
Traditional municipal solid-waste projects, however, "are conceived primarily as a means to manage and provide disposal options for a community's garbage," the report said.

While traditional municipal waste-to-energy plants receive some revenues from energy sales, they also have other revenue-raising options, such as increasing tipping fees or imposing special assessments on waste generators.
But projects like the Florida one are riskier because they rely on "an arbitrarily inflated revenue structure," lack diversity and do not serve an essential municipal purpose, Early said.
"It really does highlight the value of essentiality to a municipal project. If it's not performing an essential purpose, than you're inherently at risk," Early said.

The Florida plants are owned by the Okeelanta Power and Gator Generating Company Limited Partnerships, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy reorganization last month. The partnerships are owned by Pacific Gas & Electric Co, a unit of PG&E Corp, and Bechtel Enterprises.

The plants burn waste products from sugarcane processing. Florida's Palm Beach County issued three series of industrial development revenue bonds for the plants, totalling $288.5 million, but has no obligation toward the debt.

The bonds are in technical default because of the bankruptcy filing but no payments have been missed. An official with the partnership said there had been no decision on whether to pay the next debt service payment of about $10 million, due on July 1.
A.G. Edwards does not hold or sell any of the Palm Beach County bonds, Early said.
